title: Bina and tevuna: abstract understanding, and the applied understanding that draws it out
overview:
Chapter 2 says that *bina* has two levels. *Bina* itself is abstract understanding: a sharp grasp, a *tafsan*, can follow a deep *pilpul* and still not rule on a case, and an idea that is only understood is still a *hiyuli*, a prime matter, of which nobody yet knows the outcome. *Tevuna* is the light of *bina* spreading out, the applied understanding. It comes when the idea is absorbed, *kelita*, until it is part of how you think. Then the depth of the idea can be drawn up, like water from a deep well for the sheep, so that a man of *tevuna* (*ish tevuna*) can explain it so simply that it seems it was never deep, and can rule in a particular case.

*Tevuna* has its own depth, length and width. Its letters spell *ben u'vas*, because the love and fear are born from *tevuna*, the lower mother, and it is *tevuna* that gives them their intellect and keeps them going. The way to *tevuna* is *hisbonenus*, the double *nun*: first learn the idea and try to understand it, then see how it applies and apply it to your own life.

terms.gloss: understanding; abstract understanding, the theory of an idea

a man of *tevuna*, who can draw the depth of an idea out for others
absorbing an idea so well that it becomes part of how you think
a grasper; someone with a sharp understanding that stays in the theory
prime matter; an idea that is not yet known to have any outcome
contemplation: learning the idea and trying to understand it, the first step toward tevuna
son and daughter; the letters of *tevuna* that stand for the love and fear born from it

sections.title: Bina has two levels: understanding, and the tevuna that applies it
sections.summary: *Bina* is abstract understanding. *Tevuna* is the light of *bina* spreading out into application, and it comes only when the idea is absorbed until it is the way you think.

phrases.he: (ב) והנה ידוע שיש בבינה עצמה ב' מדרגות,
phrases.en: It's known that in *bina* itself there are two levels or two aspects within *bina*

phrases.he: בינה ותבונה,
phrases.en: and these are called *bina* and *tevuna*, which is basically, like we'll explain, abstract understanding and applied understanding

phrases.he: וענין התבונה הוא בחינת התפשטות אור הבינה
phrases.en: *tevuna* is the application of the light of *bina*, the expression of this light of *bina*

phrases.he: (כמו שכתוב בזהר דאבא ואמא תתאין הם ישראל סבא ותבונה,
phrases.en: Now like it says in the *Zohar*, that the Father and Mother, which is *chachma* and *bina*, have an upper *partzuf*, which is called *Abba* and *Ima*, and they have a lower *partzuf*, which is called *Yisroel Saba* and *tevuna*, Grandfather Israel, so referring to *Yaakov Avinu*

phrases.he: ונקרא אימא תתאה כו')
phrases.en: and *tevuna* is this idea of applied understanding, which is called the lower Mother

phrases.he: מצד קליטתה היטב בכלי המקבל
phrases.en: this ability to apply what you understand comes from really absorbing, really internalizing what you've understood *bechli hamekabel*, within your own mind

phrases.he: ההשגה דבינה,
phrases.en: so once a person really has this type of an understanding, really assimilates it into their way of thinking, they really get this experience with it

phrases.he: על כן מתפשט בה להביאה בכמה ענינים נבדלים מעצם ההשגה,
phrases.en: then you can start applying it and expressing it in many ways that are outside of the realm of that theory

phrases.he: והוא הנקרא איש תבונה,
phrases.en: and this is what's called a man of understanding

phrases.he: כמו מים עמוקים כו' איש תבונה ידלנה.
phrases.en: like it says in the *pasuk*, the deep waters, a man of *tevuna* can draw them

blocks.outOfPlace: The class opens by summing up chapter 1 (hisbonenus) before the first line of this chapter is read.
blocks.text: Before the chapter he sums up the last one. Hisbonenus is a process: you take an idea, find where it is grounded in something tangible you can see in your own life, and compare examples until you find its real depth. This also activates *chachma*, the intuition into deeper things, indirectly, since it is not something to work on directly. Doing it develops *daas*, the personal connection to the idea. Applying what you learn is a related but separate skill, and it too is developed through practice.
*Bina* has two levels, *bina* and *tevuna*. *Bina* is abstract understanding. *Tevuna* is applied understanding, the light of *bina* spreading out, the expression of that light.

Tevuna is the step where you understand an idea, recognize what you could do with it, and find particular examples of how to put the shift into practice in your own life. That is what lets you really get the benefit.

The Zohar speaks of an upper pair, *Abba* and *Ima* (*chachma* and *bina*), and a lower pair, *Yisroel Saba* and *tevuna* (Grandfather Israel, that is Yaakov Avinu in the simple reading). Tevuna is applied understanding, and it is called the lower Mother.

Tevuna comes from really absorbing the idea, internalizing it until it is in your own mind. Then the idea is not just something you learned and can repeat back. It is yours, you have mastery over it, and you can apply it.

blocks.question: What is the difference between theoretical understanding and applied understanding?
blocks.text: It is not that theory is understood differently; applied understanding is a different kind of knowledge, the knowledge of the practical problems and challenges that come up when an idea meets the world: how it works and does not work. It depends on how well the idea is integrated into your way of thinking. The student's example fits: someone who went to military school does not know what a soldier who has been in a war knows, and someone who writes a paper on a subject does not know what someone who works in the field knows. The idea also has to be considered against the conditions of the physical world where you act on it. A principle may be true in theory, but if the conditions are different when you act, you had better be ready to adjust.

Once a person really has this understanding, it becomes one with them, and it can be extended to many things outside the theory. Such a person is a man of *tevuna*. The image is a deep well: the sheep cannot get down to the water, but if it is drawn up, the sheep can drink.

blocks.title: The well and the sheep
blocks.text: You do not want people to have to climb down the well to drink. In the same way, you do not want someone to have to be the *Kohen Gadol* in the *Kodesh Kodashim* to experience G-dliness. You want the deep, essential understanding, and then you want to apply it outward.

A true leader appreciates the highest, purest truth, expressed in altruism, and sees that every person has a G-dly spark. Because he has that deep understanding, he can help people connect to G-dliness on their own level. That is the whole idea of a real leader, and what the Torah is about.

sections.title: Deep water: the depth stays hidden, and a man of tevuna draws it up
sections.summary: The depth of an idea cannot be explained or handed over directly. It must be packed into something tangible that the other person can unpack.

phrases.he: מים עמוקים הם בחינת עמקות בינה שנשאר בהעלם העצמיות,
phrases.en: the depth that talks about here is the depth of *bina* that remains hidden within the person themselves

phrases.he: ואיש תבונה דווקא ידלנה וישאבנה מן ההעלם להביאה להתפשטות בכמה אופנים שונים לרוות את המקבלים
phrases.en: and specifically somebody with *tevuna* is able to take that depth and explain it with metaphors or apply it in a way that will benefit the receivers that don't have that same depth

blocks.text: He asks what deep waters means: the depths of *bina*, which remain hidden in the self. The real depth of an understanding cannot be explained; you have to experience it directly, inside yourself, and so you cannot give it to somebody else. Even Moses cannot simply give us his level.

blocks.question: Can the inner depth of an understanding be handed to someone else?
blocks.text: Not as it is. What can be given over is a very abstract idea, and to do that it has to be brought into some tangible form that can be packaged, and the other person has to unpack it. It is like transferring data: a protocol encodes it into a medium, and it is converted more than once along the way. The student's example of a tone of voice makes the same point: it tells you how someone feels, but it is not comparable to the feeling as it exists within them. The inner state itself cannot be shared directly.

blocks.question: Is G-d designing our tangible life experiences as the means to encode what He wants us to understand?
blocks.text: He agrees with the comparison: the way to get this quality of knowledge is through applying it in the physical world. A teacher does not just want students to get an A on the test; he wants them to practice the profession for real, with patients or with numbers. So this world is basically a tutorial, one big tutorial.

The real essence of the truth is not the level that Moses reaches through his hard work, the point of *tzaddik* and the depth. What matters is that once he gets that depth, he understands it is not about arriving but about the process of growth. So he can see the essence in every person, on their level, and that is why he can lead them to bring it out.
blocks.outOfPlace: The class moves from the reading of line 3 to the point that the depth of Moses is the process of growth, said after the discussion of the encoding of truth.

blocks.title: Music, and the snob
blocks.text: Take someone who really appreciates music. A master who is a snob says that anything short of his level is worthless, and he is missing the point. Someone with real depth appreciates the joy music brings, the learning and the sharing, and even a little kid can appreciate that on his level. You should grow in your technical ability, but you should also enjoy each step and see that the essence of it is there.
blocks.outOfPlace: Off the line: after the discussion of Moses's growth, the class turns to an example from music.

sensitivity.reason: The insult word "snob" for a hypothetical master in the analogy.
sensitivity.publishable: Take someone who really appreciates music. A master says that anything short of his level is worthless, and he is missing the point. Someone with real depth appreciates the joy music brings, the learning and the sharing, and even a little kid can appreciate that on his level. You should grow in your technical ability, but you should also enjoy each step and see that the essence of it is there.

blocks.question: What does "it's about the journey, not the outcome" mean in practice?
blocks.outOfPlace: Off the line: the class moves on from line 3 to the question of growth.
blocks.text: The main value of the work is not only the result, but the broader skill set acquired along the way. Take learning Python at work. It solves the problems of one moment, but the bigger value is the skill of coding and solving whatever problems come up, and learning how to learn a new technology, because a language may not be in use in five years. The syntax is not the most important thing. Discipline in the process of learning is very valuable, but the most important thing is the growth mindset: recognizing that the essence of your life is to grow, that you always can grow, and not letting anything stop you.

blocks.title: Learning how to learn
blocks.outOfPlace: Off the line; a story told in the same class as the discussion of growth.
blocks.text: A man who had serious brain injuries as a child, who was called the kid with the broken brain, and who had very little sleep for years, overcame it all and went on to teach people how to learn. In an interview he said that if he were a genie granting one wish, he would not ask for infinite wishes. The second-best gift, he said, is the ability to learn how to learn, because then you can learn anything you need to survive. Growth presupposes that we are capable of learning and doing new things.

sensitivity.reason: A living person's childhood brain injuries and sleep history, told as an example. The name is not in the text.
sensitivity.publishable: A man who overcame serious difficulties as a child went on to teach people how to learn. In an interview he said that if he were a genie granting one wish, he would not ask for infinite wishes. The second-best gift, he said, is the ability to learn how to learn, because then you can learn anything you need to survive. Growth presupposes that we are capable of learning and doing new things.

blocks.title: Growth as the way we express G-d
blocks.outOfPlace: Off the line, after line 3 in the same class.
blocks.text: The way we express G-d is by constantly growing, creating and overcoming, not by any particular accomplishment, because none of them is great enough to matter. Wherever a person is put, the beauty of a person is that he will grow. The *tzaddik* shows how far a person can stretch the edge of accomplishment, and the *baal teshuva* who pulls himself out of hopelessness shows that the essence can always accomplish more.

blocks.question: Does the same hold for someone whose life keeps failing but who still tries?
blocks.outOfPlace: Off the line, after line 3 in the same class.
blocks.text: Even someone whose whole life is failing, who is bothered by it and tries to change, shows even more, regardless of the outcome. If it were only a matter of logic you would give up eventually. Even someone who has given up cannot stand it, because that is not who they are; they need to be doing it.

blocks.question: In what specific way does growth express G-d?
blocks.outOfPlace: Off the line, after line 3 in the same class.
blocks.text: The student suggests an answer: that G-d is infinite and not limited to any form, so that expressing that in the decision to grow shows that our self, essence or soul is not limited to its current state. The teacher says that is one way of putting it, and it is definitely one way.

blocks.title: Growth applies at every level
blocks.outOfPlace: Off the line, after line 3 in the same class.
blocks.text: Growth is a *g-dly* aspect that applies to everything: diet, fitness, finances, character, knowledge, and what people call spiritual commitments. That is why we enjoy watching people do amazing things that are pointless, like high-level snowboarding. The Torah and the mitzvos have a unique aspect, because they train a person to have real G-dly awareness, the *bechol derachecha da'eihu* of the *pasuk*. A growth mindset is a symptom of this, but it is beyond a regular growth mindset, because it comes with a perspective that goes beyond the body.

Taking the line again in the next class: the depth of *bina* is something abstract that cannot be explained directly. Only a person with *tevuna* can take that depth and explain it with metaphors, or apply it in a way that benefits those who do not have the same depth.

phrases.he: כמו הדולה מים עמוקים להשקות הצאן כו'
phrases.en: Like drawing deep water to give water to sheep

phrases.he: והוא כמו שאנו רואים בחוש, שבהיות השכל והסברא עמוקים ביותר מהכיל בהשגת אדם, הנקרא מים עמוקים כו', שהוא בחינת עומק המושג הנזכר לעיל
phrases.en: and this is what we see tangibly, that when there's an idea that's too deep and too abstract to be grasped by somebody, which is called deep waters

phrases.he: שהאורך והרוחב ממנו בא כו'
phrases.en: and this is what the length and width come from, everything is coming from this depth

phrases.he: ואיש בעל תבונה דווקא ידלנה,
phrases.en: but specifically a person with *tevuna* is able to draw it out

phrases.he: פירוש שיוציא לאור בחינת העלם העומק המושג עד שיכילנו השגת האדם, כאלו לא היה עמוק כלל,
phrases.en: He's able to bring out this depth of this idea to the point where he can explain it so it can be grasped by a person as if it wasn't deep at all

phrases.he: כמו הדולה מים עמוקים שמקרב את העומק כו'
phrases.en: this is compared to drawing water from a well, that you're taking something that was deep and making it very close

phrases.he: ולפי זה מוכרח לומר שכח התבונה הוא כח המתפשט מכח הבינה להביא עומקה לגילוי למטה למקבלים כו'
phrases.en: therefore, we must say that this idea of *tevuna* is being able to express and extend *bina* to bring its depth, so it should be revealed for the receiver in a more tangible way

blocks.title: The shepherd's well
blocks.text: Like someone drawing deep water to give the sheep a drink. Most Jewish customs work this way. Someone who understands how souls work says, you do not have to understand all of it, but if you do this, it is like medicine for your soul. Eating latkes on Hanukkah, or dressing up and shaking a gragger on Purim, connects you to the depth of the day even when you do not grasp its significance.

blocks.question: So the person who does the action, without the understanding, still benefits?
blocks.text: Yes. Such a person can get the essence of the depth. Through the action they turn on their *emunah* and their *yiras Shamayim* without having the same understanding as the teacher. Chassidus is full of this: people do not understand things on the level of the Rebbe, and they still get more benefit from it.

When an idea is too deep and too abstract for a person to grasp, it is called deep waters. This depth cannot be quantified or explained, not to this *mekabel*, and perhaps not even to yourself. Everything else, the length and the width, comes from this depth.

A person with *tevuna* is able to bring out the depth of an idea until it can be grasped by someone else, so that it seems as if it was never deep. He takes something that was abstract, difficult and obtuse and makes it relatable and practical, and then it is no longer a hard concept.

blocks.title: Drawing water from the well
blocks.text: It is like drawing water from a well: something that was deep is brought close, so that the one who needs it can use it.
The power of *tevuna* is the power that extends *bina* outward to bring its depth into view for the receivers, in a more tangible way.

sections.title: A sharp grasp that stays in the theory: the tafsan and the pilpul that yields no ruling
sections.summary: Understanding can be deep, even able to make a pilpul, and still yield no ruling and no application. Such understanding is theoretical, as an idea that is still a hiyuli.

phrases.he: מה שאין כן כשאינו איש תבונות, גם שהוא בעל השגה במוח דבינה (שנקרא תפסן בלשון העולם) יוכל להיות שהשגתו נשארת רק כמו שהיא בעצם, במוח הבינה שלו שנקרא רוח בינתו לבד, ולא יבוא ממנה שום התפשטות למטה בענין נבדל שחוץ מן עצם ההשגה כלל
phrases.en: But a person that lacks this power of *tevuna*, even if he understands something intellectually, it's possible that it remains only a theory, and it won't be expressed, you won't be able to apply it or express it to anything outside of the abstract theory

phrases.he: וגם שיש בהשגה אורך ורוחב ועומק כנזכר לעיל,
phrases.en: even though, like we said before, that in the understanding of *bina* there's a length and a width and a depth, so a person seemingly does have a length and a width, which is *hispashtus*, but it's all just within the theory

phrases.he: הכל הוא רק בעצם ההשגה,
phrases.en: It's just like within the classroom he's able to give a metaphor like this and like that, and explain it, and give examples, but it's all theoretical

phrases.he: כמו שהיא, אבל לא שיתגלה למטה בענין נבדל,
phrases.en: but not that it could be expressed in something different that's more practical and applied

phrases.he: ומכל שכן עומק המושג הרי נשאר בעומקו
phrases.en: and if even the length and width of *bina* are still theoretical, for sure the depth of the idea is completely inapplicable

phrases.he: בהעלם לעצמו, וכן האורך והרוחב, הכל בעצם ההשגה כמו שהיא, שהיא במקומה לבד
phrases.en: and so too the length and width are all just within the theory of the idea

blocks.text: A person who lacks *tevuna* can understand an idea intellectually, even be a sharp *tafsan* (what the world calls a grasper), and his understanding stays where it is, in his own *bina*. It is only a theory, and nothing from it reaches out into something separate.

We do not want our understanding of G-dliness to be a theory that exists only in the *Chassidus* books. We want it to apply to daily life, to be something you can relate to even to a random stranger, a little kid, or someone who did not study the *maamar*. They should be able to relate to it.

blocks.title: A walk outdoors
blocks.text: One of his best memories is a walk with someone who pointed out the flowers and talked about appreciating the beauty of the world: G-d could have made a world without colors, and these beautiful things are a gift that shows His love. That is real *hisbonenus*: focusing on something real in the world and connecting it to G-d, as opposed to only sitting with books that have nothing to do with the world around you. He mentions a story of two Rebbes and a leaf, which he does not tell here.

Within the classroom a person can give a metaphor like this and that, explain it and give examples, but it is all theory. The length and width of *bina* are there only in the theory, not expressed in anything practical.

blocks.title: A physics professor and an engineer
blocks.text: From his own work of teaching science: a debate between a physics professor and an electrical engineer, where those trained as engineers think about a problem in practical terms and those who think theoretically use a different way, and it seemed like a contradiction. Many things are like that. The practical skills and the understanding that serve someone in the field differ from what someone wants who only wants the theory.
If even the length and width of *bina* are still theory, the depth of the idea is completely inapplicable, and it would seem absurd that a simple person could grasp something so deep and abstract.

Professors with prestigious degrees in finance may feel jealous of a simple entrepreneur who applied the principles of business to build a plumbing business worth five million, while the Harvard professor with his PhD is worth one million. Not that net worth is the most important thing; some people find fulfillment in intellectual life, and that is fine. But there is not always an advantage in the theory alone. It has to be connected to practice.

sensitivity.reason: A mocking aside about academics: professors with doctorates are jealous of practical men, a profession named as a group.
sensitivity.publishable: A simple entrepreneur who applied the principles of business to build a plumbing business can be worth five million, while a Harvard professor with his PhD is worth one million. Not that net worth is the most important thing; some people find fulfillment in intellectual life, and that is fine. But there is not always an advantage in the theory alone. It has to be connected to practice.

blocks.text: So too the length and the width of *bina* are all within the theory of the idea, and the depth of the idea is inapplicable to anything outside it.

sections.title: Pilpul without a ruling: knowing the theory is not knowing how to apply it
sections.summary: A person can know the theory of a Talmudic debate in depth and still be unable to rule on a particular case. Applied understanding is a separate skill.

phrases.he: ודוגמא לכל זה,
הנה אנו רואים בעומק הפלפול בתלמוד וטעמים בסברות רבות כך וכך
phrases.en: Studying *Talmud* with a big *pilpul*

phrases.he: גם שבאים בהשגה דבינה,
phrases.en: even though the person understands it very well

phrases.he: אבל לא יוכלו עדיין להוציא לאור מעצם השכל איזה פסק דין חייב או זכאי כלל
phrases.en: But if you ask them, so what's the practical law based on that theory, they don't know.

phrases.he: דהיינו שלא יוכל להוציא מתוך הסברה איזה חיוב על פי זה השכל ולא איזה זכות על פי זה השכל
phrases.en: For example, they won't be able to derive, based on this logic, whether the person should be liable or whether he should be acquitted

blocks.title: Pilpul in the yeshiva
blocks.text: A rabbinic example of this is the *Gemara* study with a big *pilpul*. In his own yeshiva years, the *shiurim* were not practical, and most were splitting hairs. Ask what the practical difference is, and the answer is an example about a marriage made on condition of one reason or another. Learning for *smicha*, with the *she'eilos u'teshuvos* that relate the *sevaros* to *halacha*, is a totally different learning.

There are many people who know a lot of theory, give *shiurim* and *pilpulim*, and have no idea how it applies to actually deciding. A *rosh yeshiva* may not be able to be a *rav* who rules on an actual case, which is not necessarily a textbook case. Most cases that look like a textbook case are not, and it is a big mistake to jump to a conclusion. You have to understand the depth of the *sevaros* in order to decide.

A person can understand the *pilpul* very well, and have a deep understanding of it, but if you ask what the practical law is based on that theory, they do not know. They cannot derive from that logic whether a person should be liable or whether he should be acquitted. That is the limit of *bina*.

phrases.he: כי עדיין אין השכל והסברה רק השכלה שכליות לבד,
phrases.en: because right now it's all just a theoretical idea

phrases.he: בלתי ימצא ממנו שום התפשטות בהטיות לענין נבדל הימנה,
phrases.en: without any expression or manifestation in dictating or driving or directing something that's outside of the theory. It's not applied to real life

phrases.he: שהוא לחייב על ידה
phrases.en: which in our example would be to either have a prescription of guilt or innocence

phrases.he: או לזכות על ידה והרי זה כמו דבר ההיולי שלא נודע עדיין מה ימצא ממנה
phrases.en: and this is like an essential thing that we don't know what's going to come out from it

phrases.he: ומה יעשה בה
phrases.en: you don't know what to do with it

phrases.he: (בל"א דער מושכל אליין כמו שהוא ער קאן מיט אים נישט טאן קיין זאך ניט צו קערין לזכות או לחוב כו')
phrases.en: It's just the theory, and you can't do anything with it. You can't use it to decide, make a decision for merit or for guilt

blocks.title: The hiyuli
blocks.text: Like the *hiyuli*, the prime matter: nobody yet knows what will come out of it, or what to do with it. The idea itself, as it is, can do nothing, and cannot be used to decide for merit or for guilt. That is all *bina* itself is.

A person can understand very well and be very good at giving a *shiur*, with all kinds of examples, and it is all in the realm of theory. That is the idea of *bina*. And that is what we are trying to get at: we can learn all the *Chassidus* and all the *Kabbalah* jargon and fool ourselves that we understand because we can say so many words. Saying words does not mean understanding. It is only getting familiar with the most external part.
When people ask how to apply this to *davenen*, to their *avodah*, to their business and family, the theory does not have an answer, and they will not know.

sections.title: The power of tevuna: application to decisions, to feelings and to thought
sections.summary: *Tevuna* is the power to bring the abstract understanding out into something separate from it: a decision, a feeling in the heart, or a way of thinking it in many forms.

phrases.he: ואמנם כח התבונה שמתפשט ממוח הבינה,
phrases.en: The power of *tevuna* is the ability to apply what you learned to something practical

phrases.he: היינו מה שביכולתו להביא עצם ההשגה לבחינת התפשטות למטה ממנה בכל ענין נבדל הימנה,
phrases.en: in any sort of application in something that's outside of the theory

phrases.he: או לחיוב או לזכות או להתפעל בלב,
phrases.en: whether it's to use it to make a decision, to decide whether this is bad or good to do, whether it's going to be to influence a person's feelings about something, so they should have love and fear of *Hashem*

phrases.he: וכן להביאה במחשבה בכמה אופנים שונים כו'.
phrases.en: And also to allow them to express it in their thoughts in many ways

blocks.text: The power of *tevuna* is the ability to bring the understanding out into something separate from it: to decide whether a thing is liable or innocent, to move a person's heart, so that they have love and fear of G-d, and to express the idea in many ways in thought.

blocks.question: What does "bringing it into thought in many ways" mean?
blocks.text: He is not sure himself. It could mean many metaphors, or it could mean seeing the theme in all areas of life. Putting an idea into words, giving it a *kli*, is a kind of *machshava*: you take something abstract and find a way to express it. Finding different *meshalim*, as for a little child, is one thing. Seeing the idea in every aspect of a person's life, as in *bechol derachecha da'eihu*, is another. He thinks it is the second, but he is not positive.

phrases.he: אך לכאורה אנו רואים שיש בבינה עצמה בחינת מדות הנקרא ז׳ תחתונים דבינה, ונקרא מדות שבשכל המטה כלפי זכות או שכל מטה כלפי חוב כידוע
phrases.en: seemingly *bina* itself has *middos*, called the seven lower *sefiros* of *bina*, and called *middos* of the intellect, an intellect that leans towards innocence and towards guilt

phrases.he: היינו כמו שהמדות שבשכל הן בעצם ההשגה עדיין בהעלם
phrases.en: that's all still within the theory, that in theory you can see how this idea could lean this way or that way, but it's not creating the actual feelings

phrases.he: אבל להביא בחינת התגלותן בדבר נבדל, כמו להורות בענין מקרה דבר מה על פי השכל והסברא הזאת, להטות את המשפט של זה הענין לחסד וגבורה שבו דוקא, הרי איש תבונה דווקא יוציא לאור מן המדות שבבינה כו'
phrases.en: but to actually, you know, either to actually apply a *psak din* to a real life case as opposed to just in theory, and also to have actual feelings, so to actually give a ruling in a case, but that is already something else

blocks.question: If *bina* has *middos* of its own, the intellect that leans toward merit or guilt, why is *tevuna* needed?
blocks.text: Those *middos* of the intellect are, in the *bina* itself, still hidden in the theory. In theory you can see how an idea could lean this way or that, but it does not create the actual feelings, or a ruling in an actual case.

Applying a ruling to a real case, and having real feelings about it, requires a special kind of understanding, which is a different skill with its own practice. A professor who knows all the theory, but lacks real experience in applying it, can be an advisor, but he is not the one to decide. For that you need the experience to learn how to apply what you understand, as a judge in a *beis din* below needs to rule on a case of debt or merit.

phrases.he: ואיש תבונות היינו כח הקולט בכי טוב לעצם ההשגה,
phrases.en: the simple translation is to absorb or to internalize the idea, and that's the idea that you really don't see it as just something separate from yourself, but you really assimilate it into your way of thinking

phrases.he: על כן מתפשטת ההשגה בו לעשות ולהורות בה כמה ענינים נבדלים לגמרי
phrases.en: therefore, you can extend this idea to use it and apply it and give advice based on it in many things that are outside the theory, because it's no longer just this theoretical idea

phrases.he: וגם ביכולתו להביא את עומק בינה לידי גילוי כנזכר לעיל ודי למבין
phrases.en: such a person will be able to bring the depth over to somebody else and to impart that idea as if it wasn't deep, giving them the essence of the idea without all the theoretical understanding

blocks.text: A man of *tevuna* has absorbed the idea, so that it is part of how he thinks and he has begun to have experience with it. Then he is comfortable with it, and can extend it to things outside the theory. But he will hesitate to act on something he has only looked up without direct experience. You do not make a decision based on that.

Such a person can bring the depth to somebody else, even a child or a student, as if it wasn't deep. Sometimes people whose wisdom comes from life experience give a child something this way, and it gives him the essence of the idea, even without the theory.

phrases.he: (והיינו בחינת אבא ואמא תתאין ישראל סבא ותבונה ישראל סבא מדות דחכמה ותבונה מדות דבינה אך באין בבחינת הגילוי לחוץ ובחינת מלכות דתבונה הוא השכל הבא במחשבה הנקרא אותיות מחשבת שכל שהשכל מתלבש בה והוא בחינת כלי חיצוני למחשבה עיונית שהוא גלוי השגה דבינה עצמה מצד עצם השכל והסברא כו' ומבחינת מלכות דתבונה נמשך שרש אותיות המחשבה עצמה שנקרא לאה כו' והוא ד' רבתי דאחד)
phrases.en: and this is, like we mentioned before, the lower father and mother, which are *Yisroel Saba* and *tevuna*

blocks.text: *Chachma* and *bina* are called *Abba* and *Ima*. A *partzuf* is always a configuration of all ten *sefiros*, focused around a certain center. When all the *sefiros* are focused around *chachma* it is called *Abba*, and around *bina* it is called *Ima*. Within *chachma*, when it is theoretical understanding, it is *Abba* and *Ima*; when it is practical understanding, it is *Yisroel Saba* and *tevuna*, the grandfather of Israel, which is the *middos* of *chachma*.

This is a person at a high spiritual level who has a sense of what is holy and what is right, who is altruistic, who wants to do what is right because it is right and to know what is true because it is true. That attitude and sensitivity is the *middos* of *chachma*, going in the spirit of Grandfather Israel. The term *tzaddik* refers to someone who has that sensitivity to G-dliness that comes from practical experience. That is the *middos* of *bina*.

As it says in *Tanya*, a person at least has enough understanding to know what he should do, and so can do it without all the theory. Both can be in one person, but *tevuna* is at least knowing. A *rav* who knows the custom and how we rule may not be the best *rosh yeshiva* for a whole *pilpul* *shiur*. Learning *she'eilos u'teshuvos* is a different learning from *Gemara* with *pilpulim*, and one can be an expert in either.

*Malchus* of *tevuna* is the intellect that comes into thought, the letters of thought, a vessel for analytical thought that reveals the understanding of *bina* itself. Building the right words and jargon for an idea is creating this terminology: the analysis he meant before by putting an idea into thought in many ways. *Malchus* of *tevuna* is also the source of thought itself, *Leah*, which is simply being able to think.

sections.title: Depth, length and width: the three parts of tevuna, and how each one brings the next
sections.summary: *Tevuna* has depth (how well the idea is absorbed), length (its application to something outside it) and width (its many ways of being thought). Working on length and width is how depth grows.

phrases.he: וזהו שנקרא תבונה בן ובת כידוע,
phrases.en: and this is also connected to the idea that it says that *tevuna* is made up of the letters of *ben uvat*

phrases.he: להיות כי גם בתבונה יש ג' דברים, עומק ואורך ורוחב.
phrases.en: and again, the depth depends on the length and width, so to develop the depth you have to work on the length and width, and the more depth a person has, the more length and width they will have

phrases.he: העומק הוא עצם כח התבונה הזאת שבאותה ההשגה, כמו שהיא בשעה שקולטת אותה כו'
phrases.en: So the depth of *tevuna* is how well the person really assimilates or internalizes this idea that they're studying about

phrases.he: ובה יוכל עומק ההשגה הנזכר לעיל לבוא לגלוי, כנזכר לעיל בפסוק איש תבונה ידלנה כו'
phrases.en: and through this type of understanding a person can then express even the depth of the idea to somebody else, even in a very simple way, like to a little kid

blocks.text: *Tevuna* has three parts, depth, length and width, and its letters are *ben uvat*, son and daughter.

The depth of *tevuna* is how well a person assimilates the idea, so that he sees it not as a theory but as something he can envision in his own life. The depth depends on length and width: to develop depth, work on length and width, and the more depth you have, the more length and width you will have.
Through this understanding a person can express the depth of an idea to somebody else, even in a very simple way, to a little kid, as we said that a person of *tevuna* can draw the depth out.

phrases.he: והאורך הוא ירידתה בענין אחר הנבדל, להורות בו ולעשות מעשים רבים על ידה כו'
phrases.en: The length of *tevuna* is the ability to apply it in practical decision-making and things like that, or to have actual guidance

blocks.text: The length is the power of *tevuna* to go down into another matter and act on it: to give guidance and to do many deeds through it. Length is applying what you understood to real decisions.

phrases.he: והרוחב הוא בחינת התפשטות התבונה בעצם ההשגה, להרחיבה במחשבה בכמה רבוי אופנים שונים ולא כמו שהיא לבד כו'
phrases.en: the idea of the width of *tevuna* is taking the analysis itself, that you gain these different words and tools and things that help you think about the idea and analyze the idea, you build this kind of structure around it

blocks.text: The width of *tevuna* is the spreading of the understanding in many forms, so that it is not only as it is. It helps the analysis: you gain words and tools that let you think about the idea, and build a structure around it, which is why a good teacher has a whole wisdom in developing teaching aids.

blocks.title: Learning a maamar in your own life
blocks.text: Take a *maamar* and look at how the Rebbe's letters apply its ideas to day-to-day life, even to money matters. Then ask how you could apply it to your own life, and then live it and experience it. The more a person practices that, the more he will see whatever he learns as something he can use.

blocks.question: Do those two examples map to width and to length?
blocks.text: Not quite. The letter is an example of length, a length you get from somebody else. Then you also need to do the work yourself, practicing how to apply what you are learning to your own life. That is also length.

blocks.question: Is it the case that whenever you have at least two lengths, you have gained width?
blocks.text: If they are different, you start to get width. The more ways you can see that an idea applies in different aspects of life, the more width you build, and especially when you understand the idea itself in different ways based on those applications.

sections.title: Ben u'vas: the emotions are born from tevuna, the lower mother
sections.summary: The love and fear are born from *tevuna*, the lower mother, and not from *bina* itself, the upper mother. Real feelings come when the theory is brought into the real world.

phrases.he: ומה שכלולה התבונה מב''ן וב''ת, היינו מה שמתבונה דוקא יולדו המדות בגלוי מהות בפני עצמם,
phrases.en: and this idea that *tevuna* is made up of, includes *ben u'vas*, includes the love and fear

phrases.he: כי מבינה עצמה לא היו תולדות המדות
phrases.en: just the theoretical understanding, you can learn to understand it very well, it's not really going to change how you feel

phrases.he: אף על פי שנקרא אם הבנים כו' (אבל היא אימא עילאה)
phrases.en: even though we say *bina* is the mother of the children, so the understanding is ultimately going to be the source of your love and fear, but it's the upper mother

phrases.he: מה שאין כן התבונה נקרא אימא תתאה להוליד המדות,
phrases.en: but *tevuna* is called the lower mother, which is specifically the part of *bina* that relates to giving birth and creating these feelings

phrases.he: והוא בחינת ב''ן וב''ת, אהבה ויראה, שבאים בהתכללות בתבונה דוקא, שהיא בחינת התפשטות אור הבינה למטה כנזכר לעיל
phrases.en: when you learn something, if you think about how it relates to you, that type of thinking is going to actually start creating those feelings, as opposed to just a theoretical understanding; if you plug that into the *tevuna*, that will supercharge it

blocks.text: Every Jew has natural feelings: a natural love for G-dliness, a natural curiosity and love of learning, a natural desire to contribute and help people. These can stay hidden as a love that is concealed. To reveal them as feelings that have a life of their own, and are not just something you know you should do, a person has to be passionate about it, and that comes from *tevuna*.

Just from the theoretical understanding, a person can understand very well and it will not change how he feels. Even so, *bina* is called the mother of the children, and it is the ultimate source of love and fear, but it is the upper mother. It is like a father and mother who have a life of their own apart from the children, and a different aspect of themselves gives birth to and raises them. That is the idea of *Yisroel Saba* and *tevuna*.

When you learn something and see how it applies to you, that creates real feelings, and that supercharges *tevuna* with more depth. If you do not plug it in, the understanding is like a head detached from the body. That is the idea of *Amalek*, which is like cutting off the head. The love and fear are included in *tevuna* and brought out from it when you see how the theory, which is the outflow of *bina*, applies to the real world, and that is where you have real feelings, because something matters to you in your life.

phrases.he: וגם לזה הטעם בחינת המוחין שבמדות נמשך מבחינת התבונה (וכמו שכתוב יהו״ה בחכמה יסד ארץ, דאבא יסד ברתא כו'
phrases.en: this is also why the intellect of the emotions, the part of the intellect that's able to guide the emotions, comes from *tevuna* also

phrases.he: כונן שמים בתבונה, שמים הן בחינת המדות, אש מים כידוע
phrases.en: So it says that G-d founded the earth with wisdom, because *chachma* is the source of *Malchus*, but it says He maintains and sets up the heavens with *tevuna*. *Shamayim* is the idea of the *middos*, the word *shamayim* is a contraction of *eish* and *mayim*, fire and water, which is the idea of *chesed* and *gevura*

phrases.he: וכן ובתבונה יתכונן, שהוא בחינת קיום המדות בבחינת המוחין דתבונה שבהם,
phrases.en: so too it says in a *pasuk* that with *tevuna* they are maintained, which is the idea of the *middos* being kept, in order for a person's love and fear to remain, they have to have this intellect that drives them and keeps them going

phrases.he: כי התבונה כמו ממוצע להביא מוחין מבחינת מדות דבינה במדות שבלב
phrases.en: because *tevuna* is like an intermediary to bring the theoretical understanding of *bina* to the feelings in the heart

phrases.he: שזהו כמו כח ההבאה בענין הנבדל, שהוא עיקר ענין התבונה כנזכר לעיל
phrases.en: which is very similar to this idea of applying what you learn to something practical, it's also applying it to your own feelings. Which, as we said before, is the whole theme of *tevuna*

blocks.text: The intellect that guides the emotions also comes from *tevuna*. The verse says G-d founded the earth with *chachma*, because *chachma* is the source of *Malchus*, but He maintains and sets up the heavens with *tevuna*. The heavens are the *middos*, and the word *shamayim* is a contraction of fire and water, *chesed* and *gevura*.

*Tevuna* is what maintains the *middos*. A person can be inspired, but if the inspiration comes only from outside, it goes away. When the feeling comes from a person's own understanding, it is like a candle that burns and stays with him wherever he goes. *Tevuna* is the intermediary that brings the theoretical understanding of *bina* into the feelings of the heart, which is the power of applying an idea to your own feelings.

sections.title: The two nuns: hisbonenus is the double nun that brings bina out into tevuna
sections.summary: *Bina* has a bent *nun*, its width, and a straight *nun*, its length, and the length is included in the width. The double *nun* of *hisbonenus* is the intermediary between *bina* and *tevuna*: first learn the idea and try to understand it.

phrases.he: וידוע גם כן שיש נו''ן כפופה ונו''ן פשוטה בבינה,
phrases.en: And so within *bina* itself, there are two types of learning which correspond to the bent *nun* and the straight *nun*

phrases.he: להיות נו''ן כפופה הוא הרוחב ונו''ן פשוטה הוא האורך
phrases.en: So we see that the width and the length get connected

phrases.he: ונ' המלוי שלו בנ' פשוטה
phrases.en: the spelling of the bent *nun* is with the long *nun*

phrases.he: מה שאין כן בשאר מילוי האותיות
phrases.en: that implies that when you have the width, that automatically is going to bring the length, and that's not the case with other letters

phrases.he: כי האורך נכלל ברוחב
phrases.en: because the length is really included within the width

phrases.he: וכך הוא בתבונה,
phrases.en: and so too with *tevuna*

phrases.he: ואמנם נון הכפל בענין הנקרא התבוננות, כמו עמי לא התבונן וכו',
phrases.en: we also see a double *nun* in *hisbonenus*, which can also imply a long *nun*, as we see in the word *hisbonen*, the prophet complains that my nation doesn't *hisbonen*, and it's a bent *nun* and then a long *nun*

phrases.he: שזהו בחינת פנימית בינה הנקרא עיון, לעמוד על דבר כו'
phrases.en: that's the inner *bina*, which is *iyun*, to dwell on a matter

phrases.he: שנקרא בינה שבבינה, הוא ממוצע בין בינה לתבונה
phrases.en: this is the intermediary between *bina* and *tevuna*

phrases.he: על ידי הנו''ן פשוטה, שמחמתו נקרא התבוננות כו' ודי למבין:
phrases.en: So first it starts off with *hisbonenus*, just learning the idea and trying to understand it

blocks.text: Within *bina* there are two kinds of learning, which correspond to the bent *nun* and the straight *nun*. The bent *nun* is the width and the straight *nun* is the length. The *nun* is the only letter spelled this way, in both its bent and long forms. *Mem* has a closed and an open form, but no long form.

The spelling of the bent *nun* is with the straight *nun*. So when you have the width, the length is automatically brought with it, which is not the case with other letters. That is why the length is included in the width, and so too in *tevuna*.

To gain the ability to apply an idea, you start by learning it in a book, as the theory. But while you learn the theory, you try to think about it this way: how could I apply this, what examples of it are in my life? That is the process of width, and it trains you to have the idea direct your daily life in a practical way.

The double *nun* in *hisbonenus* can imply a long *nun*, as in the word *hisbonen*, which the prophet uses when he complains that the nation does not *hisbonen*. That is the inner aspect of *bina*, which is *iyun*, to dwell on a matter.

*Bina sheb'bina* is the intermediary between *bina* and *tevuna*, by the straight *nun*, and so it is called *hisbonenus*. First you learn the idea and try to understand it. Once the theory has depth and clarity, you can work on *tevuna*: see different examples of how the idea applies, and then apply it to real life.

The point of this chapter: since we do not want our understanding to remain theory, we have to study with the purpose of moving toward *tevuna*, applied understanding. This is not magic and it is not a gift only some people have. Study *Gemara* the way you do when learning for *smicha*, looking for how it applies to something practical, rather than a pure *iyun shiur* with the same *pilpulim* and *mefarshim* and nothing practical. It will train you to see everything you learn as practical and related to *maaseh*. Ask what examples of it are in your life, how you would look at it differently before and after learning it, and what difference that makes.

blocks.question: Is this the difference between a *maskil* and an *oved*?
blocks.text: In terms of approach, yes. A proper *maskil* is also an *oved*, and a proper *oved* is also a *maskil*. The main difference is direction, where they start. A *maskil* starts with the theory and tries to bring it to practice. An *oved* starts with something practical, his self-improvement, and then looks to the theory for guidance, so it is grounded from the beginning.

blocks.title: The Vilna Gaon and the Alter Rebbe
blocks.text: Why did the Vilna Gaon not want to meet the Alter Rebbe? The Gaon had studied *Kabbalah* from many masters as a young man, while the Alter Rebbe had essentially one teacher, and he relied on him. The explanation he was given is that the Alter Rebbe was a *posek* and the Gaon was not, so if the Alter Rebbe came and said a *psak*, the Gaon would have had to listen. He says he does not know what was in either one's head, and that he is passing on the story as it was told to him. He says the story fits what the class is learning.
